classification.difficultyReason: Count the unit cells within each marked rectangle, optionally organising the count by rows, and report the total in square centimetres as instructed.

content.prompt: Find the area of each of the rectangles on the grid below by counting the number of squares. Imagining that the figures below have been drawn on $1\text{ cm}^2$ grid paper.

spec.description: An 18-column, 10-row square grid with labelled rectangles in their original relative positions. A blank-grid template cannot express the four positioned shaded regions and labels. Ordinary outlines are black; light blue identifies the regions to count.
spec.mathematics: Coordinates measured right and down from the top-left: a=(1,1) to (4,5); b=(8,1) to (14,5); c=(16,1) to (17,9); d=(2,6) to (12,9). Every cell represents 1 square centimetre.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied grid, regions and labels are visible; no areas are supplied.

answer.worked: There are 4 rows of 3 unit squares, giving 12 squares. Each square has area $1\text{ cm}^2$, so the area is $12\text{ cm}^2$.
There are 4 rows of 6 unit squares, giving 24 squares. Each square has area $1\text{ cm}^2$, so the area is $24\text{ cm}^2$.
There are 8 rows of 1 unit square, giving 8 squares. Each square has area $1\text{ cm}^2$, so the area is $8\text{ cm}^2$.
There are 3 rows of 10 unit squares, giving 30 squares. Each square has area $1\text{ cm}^2$, so the area is $30\text{ cm}^2$.
